title: New operational assets likely to bolster Dialog's growth into FY27 | The Star
description:
Dialog delivered a record core net profit of RM604mil for FY26, surging 43% year-on-year (y-o-y) and fully matching consensus expectations.
In a note, CGSI Research said excluding a one-off RM31mil inventory write-down, fourth-quarter core net profit rose 35% quarter-on-quarter (q-o-q) to RM193mil.
Meanwhile, MBSB Research has taken a more bullish stand, maintaining a “buy” call and setting a higher target price of RM2.57.
It adjusted FY27 and FY28 earnings forecasts upward by 5% and 3%, respectively.
Hong Leong Investment Bank (HLIB) Research also maintains a “buy” recommendation on Dialog with a sum-of-parts derived target price of RM2.52.
text:
PETALING JAYA: CGS International (CGSI) Research has maintained its “add” rating on Dialog Group Bhd with an unchanged target price of RM2.46, a 25.5% upside, following stellar financial results for the financial year ended June 30, 2026 (FY26).

Dialog delivered a record core net profit of RM604mil for FY26, surging 43% year-on-year (y-o-y) and fully matching consensus expectations.

In a note, CGSI Research said excluding a one-off RM31mil inventory write-down, fourth-quarter core net profit rose 35% quarter-on-quarter (q-o-q) to RM193mil.

“Total dividends for the year increased to 4.7 sen per share, up from 3.1 sen in FY25, representing a 45% payout ratio,” the research house said.

The performance was driven by higher upstream margins as crude oil prices averaged US$97 per barrel, up 23% q-o-q, alongside stronger downstream contributions from major plant turnaround work at the Kerteh Integrated Petrochemical Complex, and robust project execution.

CGSI Research explained that growth is projected to continue into FY27, backed by new operational assets

These include first contributions from the Cendramas brownfield asset (September 2026) and Baram gas cluster (early 2027), the opening of the 150,000 cubic m storage capacity expansion at Dialog Group’s Langsat 3 facility in September 2026 under a six-year take-or-pay lease, and strong tailwinds for its tank terminal operations as global energy security concerns drive storage demand to stable South-East Asian hubs.

Meanwhile, MBSB Research has taken a more bullish stand, maintaining a “buy” call and setting a higher target price of RM2.57. It adjusted FY27 and FY28 earnings forecasts upward by 5% and 3%, respectively.

Beyond the Langsat 3 project, MBSB Research highlights two major upcoming developments at Pengerang Deepwater Terminals (PDT); 272,000 m3 for Pengerang Biorefinery with targeted completion in first-half calendar year 2028, and the 614,000 cubic m under a long-term agreement with BP Singapore (targeted completion mid-2028), as well as over 202.3 ha reserved for future hub developments.

MBSB Research provides specific timelines for new upstream assets, including first hydrocarbon at the Salbiah gas field by the second quarter of FY27 (2Q27) and ongoing pre-development studies for the RAJA and Mutiara Clusters.

It further states that Dialog’s strategic transition into green infrastructure such as sustainable aviation fuel or SAF storage, biofuel terminals, and the PETRONAS Gas liquified natural gas-driven Air Separation Unit as key long-term catalysts.

Hong Leong Investment Bank (HLIB) Research also maintains a “buy” recommendation on Dialog with a sum-of-parts derived target price of RM2.52.

This represents a potential capital upside of 28.6% over the current trading price of RM1.96, complemented by an expected 2% dividend yield, giving a total expected return of 30.6%.

title: EESN Discussion - Sustainable Aviation Fuel for the Airline Energy Transition
description:
Click here to learn more and register
Do you like (or hate) to fly - to vacations, visit friends and family, or for business? But flying takes the most energy per mile (and passenger) travelled. Jet fuel, a dense energy fuel, is well matched to providing the large amount of energy a 90 MW engine needs for the large planes that fly long distances. Recent geo-political events have shown that the conventional supply is subject to all the risks of other world market fuels..
Are there good options for the industry to reduce its pollution and decarbonize operations?  Currently, most producers convert waste food grease to Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), but the amount of grease and the limited bio-refineries can only provide less than 1% of the aviation need. 
Irshad Ahmed MBA '12, founder and CEO of Avalon BioEnergy, will first present the opportunity and challenges of scaling up production of this fuel. He will talk about the company's innovative technology and business approach to making SAF from waste agricultural materials and crops that can grow on land unsuitable for food production
Join this discussion led by Irshad on the pros and cons of SAF as a promising option for the aviation energy transiition. (More background on the decarbonization challenges for the aviation industry in this podcast on the jet fuel crisis, hosted by Christiana Figueres, co-chair of the Paris Agreement COP )
We invite material product engineers, business planners, fuel supply and operational professionals and other interested alums to brainstorm and join the discussion of issues posed by this emerging industry. As the leader of the EESN Climate Business and Innovation group (CBI), Irshad will be listening for other ideas to discuss or innovative tech to pass along to the EESN Tech Group.

text:
Nextchem, the sustainable technology solutions arm of MAIRE, has been awarded licensing, a process design package (PDP) and engineering services for the syngas section of Project Lion, a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) project in the Burdekin region of North Queensland, Australia, the group said on 17 August.

The award was made to Nextchem’s subsidiary MyRechemical by SKY Renewables Burdekin Pty Ltd, an Australian project development company focused on SAF production. It is subject to a notice to proceed, with the exception of certain engineering services, MAIRE said.

The project will use locally available sugarcane residues as feedstock to produce purified chemical grade syngas through Nextchem’s proprietary NX Circular gasification technology, the company said. The syngas will then be converted into SAF and renewable diesel through third-party solutions. At full operational scale, Project Lion has the potential to produce up to 125,000 tonnes of sustainable aviation fuel a year, according to MAIRE.

By valorising sugarcane tops and trash — residual biomass that is often burned in the field — the project demonstrates how NX Circular gasification enables the transformation of agricultural residues into a valuable intermediate for low-carbon fuels, while supporting a more sustainable use of local biomass resources, the company said.

“This award confirms the strategic relevance of Nextchem’s proprietary technologies in enabling the development of sustainable fuels from renewable and residual feedstocks. We are proud to contribute to a project of this kind in Australia, a geography of growing importance in the evolution of the industry and an important area for the diversification of our portfolio. By leveraging our gasification technology, we can support the conversion of locally available sugarcane residues into low-carbon fuels, combining circular carbon solutions with the decarbonisation needs of aviation,” said Fabio Fritelli, managing director of Nextchem.

MAIRE said the award expands the group’s presence to a new geographical region.

MAIRE describes itself as a leading engineering group providing technology solutions and project execution in the downstream segment of energy services, as well as in the chemicals and fertilisers industries. It operates through two business units — Integrated Engineering and Construction (E&C) Solutions and Sustainable Technology Solutions, the latter active in sustainable fertilisers, low carbon energy vectors, and innovative materials and circular solutions — and employs approximately 10,800 people across operations in around 50 countries. The group is listed on the Milan Stock Exchange under the ticker MAIRE.

MAIRE classified the announcement as non-price sensitive.

title: Coconut Oil Jet Fuel Matches Kerosene's Efficiency in Engine Tests - StudyFinds
description:
Rather than stopping at production, the team took the next step and burned the fuel in a small jet engine, measuring both engine performance and exhaust emissions.
A Greener Way to Make Coconut Oil Jet Fuel Most SAF production routes involve intense industrial processes, including high-temperature refining steps that drain energy out of the fuel’s lifecycle before a single flight takes place.
Inside the Engine: How Coconut Oil Jet Fuel Actually Performs Researchers tested the fuel in a small commercial jet engine capable of reaching speeds up to 130,000 rotations per minute.
What Comes Out of the Exhaust Emissions are where coconut oil-based jet fuel shows some of its most encouraging results.
Challenges Still Ahead for Coconut Oil Jet Fuel Several practical hurdles stand between this biofuel and routine use in aircraft.
text:
Coconut oil has long had a place in kitchens and beauty products, but researchers are now making a serious case for putting it in jet engines. New research found that aviation biofuel made from coconut oil can power a small jet engine about as efficiently as traditional jet fuel, with lower unburned hydrocarbon emissions, though the blends burn more fuel and emit slightly more carbon monoxide.

Aviation accounts for a meaningful share of global carbon dioxide emissions, and pressure on the industry to find cleaner fuel options has intensified in recent years. The International Civil Aviation Organization has identified sustainable aviation fuel, commonly called SAF, as the single most effective strategy available for cutting aviation’s carbon footprint. But many current methods for producing SAF are themselves energy-hungry and costly, which chips away at the environmental benefit. The new study, published in the journal Fuel, zeroes in on a production approach designed to sidestep that problem entirely, using a technique that requires far less energy to make the fuel in the first place.

Researchers at Osaka Metropolitan University tested biofuels made from coconut oil through what they call a “co-solvent method,” a process that mixes acetone with alcohol and coconut oil to produce high-purity biofuel without the intense heat and pressure required by conventional production methods. Rather than stopping at production, the team took the next step and burned the fuel in a small jet engine, measuring both engine performance and exhaust emissions.

A Greener Way to Make Coconut Oil Jet Fuel

Most SAF production routes involve intense industrial processes, including high-temperature refining steps that drain energy out of the fuel’s lifecycle before a single flight takes place. The co-solvent method works differently. By adding acetone to a mixture of alcohol and coconut oil, normally incompatible liquids blend uniformly and react completely at relatively low temperatures, producing biofuel with purity levels exceeding 97%.

Coconut itself offers a practical advantage as a raw material. Roughly 30% of the coconut is discarded after extracting its internal moisture during processing. This study used oil from material the researchers describe as discarded and non-edible, including the large seeds and leftover flesh, so the fuel draws on parts of the crop that would otherwise go to waste. The process also produces biodiesel suitable for vehicles and marine vessels, plus high-quality glycerin as a byproduct.

Two types of biofuel were produced and tested: one made using methanol and another made using ethanol. Both are plant-based fuels commonly studied for diesel engines, but this research examined their behavior in a jet engine, a question that has received comparatively little scientific attention.

Inside the Engine: How Coconut Oil Jet Fuel Actually Performs

Researchers tested the fuel in a small commercial jet engine capable of reaching speeds up to 130,000 rotations per minute. Researchers blended the biofuels with conventional kerosene at ratios of 10%, 30%, and 50% biofuel by volume, then ran the engine across a range of speeds. Measurements included fuel consumption, engine efficiency, and exhaust concentrations of four pollutants: unburned hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and nitric oxide.

In terms of fuel efficiency, the biofuel blends required more fuel to produce the same amount of thrust. At 80,000 rotations per minute, a 50% methanol-based blend consumed about 16.8% more fuel than pure kerosene, while the ethanol-based version consumed about 19.6% more. This is largely because the biofuels carry less energy per kilogram than kerosene, so more must be burned to maintain the same output level.

Despite burning more fuel by weight, the blends converted heat into usable work at rates comparable to pure kerosene. At 100,000 rotations per minute, the thermal efficiency of the highest biofuel blend differed from pure kerosene by a small margin, and thrust output remained consistent across all blend ratios tested.

What Comes Out of the Exhaust

Emissions are where coconut oil-based jet fuel shows some of its most encouraging results. Increasing the proportion of biofuel in the blend consistently reduced unburned hydrocarbon emissions. At a 50% blend ratio, hydrocarbon concentrations in the exhaust dropped by roughly 5% to 40% compared to pure kerosene, depending on engine speed. Researchers said the drop was likely tied in part to fuel composition, since the coconut-derived biofuels contain none of the ring-shaped, aromatic hydrocarbon molecules present in conventional jet fuel.

Carbon dioxide emissions remained at levels consistent with pure kerosene across all blending ratios tested. While higher biofuel content increased total fuel consumption, the CO2 in the exhaust did not rise proportionally. Researchers say that pattern may point to some unburned biofuel leaving the engine, a question they flagged for future investigation.

Carbon monoxide emissions, a product of incomplete combustion, did increase modestly at higher blend ratios. A 50% blend produced roughly 3% to 17% more carbon monoxide than pure kerosene depending on engine speed. Researchers linked this to the biofuels being harder to ignite than kerosene and carrying less energy, both of which can create fuel-rich zones inside the combustion chamber where oxygen runs short.

Nitric oxide emissions, which can contribute to ozone depletion at high altitudes, were broadly comparable between the biofuel blends and pure kerosene. A 30% methanol-based blend showed nitric oxide concentrations 20% to 30% lower than pure kerosene across all operating conditions tested, a result the authors say requires further study to fully explain.

Challenges Still Ahead for Coconut Oil Jet Fuel

Several practical hurdles stand between this biofuel and routine use in aircraft. Coconut-derived biofuels absorb atmospheric moisture during storage, are susceptible to gradual oxidation over time, and can cause slight corrosion of metal components. Stainless steel exposed to the methanol-based version showed signs of rust after one to two weeks. The authors note that extended testing over months to years is needed, and that antioxidant additives and better-sealed storage containers are worth investigating.

Oxygen content in the biofuels also falls outside current international certification standards for aviation fuel, meaning additional chemical processing would be required before these fuels could fly in commercial aircraft. A hydrogenation treatment could bring oxygen levels into compliance, though the researchers acknowledge that process would reduce fuel yield.

International routes may also facilitate trade, investment and conference travel, while domestic routes improve connectivity between regional economies.
text:
American Airlines Dallas routes are changing the way people travel from Texas. During 2026 American Airlines Dallas routes will link Dallas Fort Worth International Airport to Athens, Zurich, Lincoln and Roanoke. These new American Airlines Dallas routes are important because they connect trips to Europe with year-round flights to smaller American cities. Athens and Zurich help grow the reach of Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. At the time Lincoln and Roanoke will find it much easier to reach the big network at the hub. These new flights are also coming at a time when Dallas Fort Worth International Airport is spending a lot of money to build facilities. This work will help the airport handle people and stay a top place for travel, around the world.

American Airlines Dallas routes create four distinct travel opportunities

American Airlines’ 2026 network programme has introduced four routes involving Dallas Fort Worth International Airport that collectively extend the Texas hub’s reach across Europe and the United States. The additions connect DFW with Athens in Greece, Zurich in Switzerland, Lincoln in Nebraska and Roanoke in Virginia.

Although all four services form part of American’s wider 2026 expansion, they serve different markets and operate under different schedules. Athens and Zurich are long-haul seasonal routes designed around summer demand, international tourism and major connecting flows. Lincoln and Roanoke are year-round domestic services intended to provide consistent regional access to American’s largest hub.

The official programme therefore represents more than a simple collection of new flights. It combines international destination development, domestic network integration and hub-based connecting opportunities.

American announced the two European services in August 2025. The airline subsequently announced the domestic additions in December 2025 as part of a package of 15 new routes planned for 2026. All four had entered service by June 2026.

According to American Airlines, the relevant route details were:

American’s initial international announcement assigned a Boeing 787-8 to Athens and a Boeing 777-200 to Zurich. Its official launch announcement later said the services operated using a mix of Boeing 777-300ER and Boeing 777-200ER aircraft. Travellers should therefore check the aircraft displayed for their individual flight rather than assume that one type will operate every departure.

Why the four routes should not be treated as identical

The phrase four new American Airlines routes from Dallas can obscure an important distinction. The flights do not share one launch date, duration, frequency or strategic purpose.

The DFW–Athens service gives Texas travellers a nonstop gateway to Greece during the peak European holiday season. The Zurich link provided a limited summer connection timed partly around major international travel demand in 2026. Lincoln gained two daily flights, creating multiple opportunities for connections through DFW. Roanoke received one daily service linking Virginia’s Blue Ridge region with Texas and American’s broader domestic and international network.

This distinction matters to travellers. Seasonal routes require closer attention to operating dates. A flight available during July may not remain available in autumn. Year-round routes offer greater continuity, but schedules can still change according to operational and commercial requirements.

The central traveller benefit is not limited to direct journeys between each pair of cities. DFW functions as a major connecting hub. Passengers originating in Nebraska or Virginia can use the new flights to reach numerous destinations through one itinerary. Likewise, travellers arriving from Greece or Switzerland can connect across American’s US network, subject to immigration procedures, baggage requirements and the published schedule.

Athens gives Texas travellers a direct route into Greece

A new nonstop option from DFW

American launched its Dallas Fort Worth to Athens flight on 21 May 2026. Its official international route announcement described the service as daily and seasonal.

The airline presented Athens as one of Europe’s most sought-after destinations and highlighted its combination of history, food and access to the Greek islands. The route also made DFW American’s fifth US gateway offering nonstop Athens service in its announced summer programme.

For North Texas residents, a nonstop journey can remove the need to connect at another US or European airport. That can reduce the number of boarding processes and airport transfers within an itinerary. It also creates a simpler proposition for travellers carrying checked baggage or planning a multi-generational holiday.

The route’s significance extends beyond the Dallas metropolitan area. American’s DFW network brings passengers into the hub from cities across the United States. Travellers from those markets can connect at DFW and continue to Athens on the same airline network.

American stated that it planned a record 18 daily summer flights from the United States to Italy and Greece across its wider operation. The Athens addition therefore formed part of a larger strategy to increase capacity towards established Mediterranean destinations.

Athens is both a destination and an onward gateway

Athens offers a deep concentration of cultural and archaeological attractions, including the Acropolis and its surrounding historic landscape. It also acts as an important entry point for travellers continuing to other parts of mainland Greece or to the islands.

However, a direct DFW flight should not be confused with direct connectivity to every Greek destination. Visitors continuing to an island may need a domestic flight, ferry, road transfer or a combination of services. Connection time should account for immigration, baggage collection where required and movement between terminals or transport modes.

The practical value of the route depends on the traveller’s final destination. A visitor staying in Athens receives the clearest benefit from nonstop access. A passenger continuing elsewhere still avoids an intermediate transatlantic connection, even though a domestic transfer may remain necessary.

Tour operators can use the service to construct open-jaw or multi-centre itineraries, combining Athens with islands, archaeological sites and regional cities. Business travellers also gain a direct link between North Texas and the Greek capital during the operating season.

Greece’s tourism strength supports the route

Greece’s established tourism economy provides a strong backdrop for additional transatlantic capacity. Official tourism statistics consistently identify international travel as an important component of the national economy.

Demand is highly seasonal. Summer draws visitors towards Athens, coastal resorts and islands, increasing pressure on accommodation, transport and major attractions. The route’s seasonal structure reflects this pattern by concentrating capacity when leisure demand is strongest.

Travellers should book popular ferries, island flights and accommodation early during peak periods. They should also allow enough time between independently ticketed services. Airlines generally do not carry the same rebooking obligations for a separately purchased onward journey as they do for protected connections issued under one ticket.

The new route can also support visits outside Greece’s most famous island destinations. Athens provides access to cultural sites and mainland regions that may benefit from wider international connectivity when travellers distribute their spending beyond a single location.

Zurich links DFW with a major Swiss aviation gateway

The seasonal service had a defined end date

American’s Dallas Fort Worth to Zurich route launched on 21 May 2026 and was officially scheduled to operate until 4 August 2026. This makes the timing especially important.

As of the verification date of 4 August 2026, the published seasonal window had reached its final day. The route should therefore not be described as a permanent, year-round link. Any future return would require confirmation through American’s official timetable or a new airline announcement.

The service complemented an existing winter-seasonal pattern by adding a limited summer operation. American said it would provide the only nonstop link between DFW and Zurich during the specified period.

Zurich is valuable for several types of traveller. It is Switzerland’s largest city, an important financial centre and a gateway to the country’s rail network. Visitors can use it as a base for urban tourism or continue to other Swiss destinations by train.

The route also had relevance for travellers moving in the opposite direction. Swiss visitors could reach Texas directly and connect through DFW to other American destinations.

Switzerland recorded strong accommodation demand

Official Swiss Federal Statistical Office data showed that the country’s hotel sector registered a record 43.9 million overnight stays in 2025, an increase of approximately 1.1 million nights over 2024.

Across hotels and supplementary accommodation, Switzerland recorded 62 million overnight stays in 2025, representing growth of 3.2 per cent. Foreign visitors accounted for 29.1 million of those nights, up 4.9 per cent.

These figures demonstrate the scale of Switzerland’s visitor economy, although they do not measure demand specifically for the DFW route. Route-level performance should not be inferred from national accommodation totals without airline booking or passenger information.

The official statistics nevertheless provide context. Zurich connects visitors with a mature tourism market supported by hotels, rail infrastructure, mountain destinations, conference activity and international business travel.

For the first half of 2026, Switzerland’s hotels recorded 20.3 million overnight stays, according to the Federal Statistical Office. That represented a decrease of 0.7 per cent, or approximately 143,000 nights, compared with the corresponding period.

The modest decline demonstrates why new air capacity should be assessed carefully rather than automatically presented as evidence of unlimited tourism growth. Aviation access can support demand, but currency movements, accommodation prices, economic conditions and traveller preferences also affect bookings.

Rail connectivity increases Zurich’s usefulness

Zurich Airport is integrated with Switzerland’s rail system, allowing travellers to continue towards destinations such as Lucerne, Bern, Basel and Alpine resort regions. The efficiency of this onward network enhances the value of Zurich as an arrival point.

Visitors should still confirm the last available train when arriving late and allow time for immigration and baggage collection. Rail tickets, seat reservations and fare conditions vary depending on the journey.

For tourism businesses, the service created opportunities to package urban and Alpine experiences around a direct Texas connection. For corporate travellers, it temporarily reduced the need to connect elsewhere when travelling between North Texas and Switzerland’s main commercial centre.

Its limited operating period, however, means tourism organisations and travel sellers should avoid marketing the route as currently available without checking the live schedule. Accuracy is especially important after 4 August 2026.

Lincoln gains year-round access to American’s largest hub

Twice-daily flights provide schedule choice

The Dallas Fort Worth to Lincoln route began on 4 June 2026 with two daily flights operated using Bombardier CRJ-700 regional aircraft. American announced the route as a year-round service.

Twice-daily frequency provides more utility than a single departure because passengers may have a choice of connection windows. It can also improve itinerary flexibility if one flight does not align with an onward service.

Lincoln Airport states that American’s service gives local passengers access through the airline’s wider network. American said its hubs collectively connect customers with more than 350 destinations served by the airline, while its airline partnerships extend access further.

The route also supports inbound travel to Nebraska’s capital. Lincoln attracts government, university, sporting, business and leisure traffic. The city is home to the Nebraska state government and the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, creating demand that extends beyond conventional holidays.

For Texans, the nonstop link opens a direct path to Lincoln without requiring a road transfer from another regional airport. For Nebraska residents, DFW offers access to destinations in the southern and western United States, Mexico, Latin America and beyond.

Nebraska tourism has measurable economic importance

Official Nebraska Tourism Commission information shows that tourism supported more than 42,000 jobs in 2024. State lodging tax revenue exceeded US$8 million, while 80 per cent of out-of-state visitors stayed in paid accommodation.

The commission’s tourism statistics also show that visitors generated US$323.3 million in state and local tax revenue in 2024. It estimated that replacing this contribution through resident taxation would have cost approximately US$392 per Nebraska household.

Earlier official figures recorded US$4.6 billion in visitor spending during 2023, up from US$3.5 billion in 2019. That represented growth of 29.4 per cent across the period.

These statewide figures cannot be attributed to one air route. The Lincoln–DFW service is new, and a credible assessment of its incremental effect would require passenger origin-and-destination data, load factors, visitor surveys and spending information.

Nevertheless, improved air access can support the conditions needed for tourism growth. It makes the destination easier to sell, widens the range of feasible short trips and gives meetings or events planners another route option.

The route is important for outbound travellers too

Tourism impact is often discussed only in terms of visitors arriving at a destination. The Lincoln route also matters to Nebraska residents leaving the state.

A hub connection can make international and domestic journeys more practical by reducing the need to drive to a distant airport. This can be especially valuable for travellers carrying luggage, families and passengers whose itineraries begin or end outside major metropolitan areas.

American specifically highlighted one-stop access from Lincoln to international destinations including Athens, Cancún, Rome and São Paulo. Availability depends on dates and connection schedules, but the examples illustrate how the domestic route plugs Lincoln into a much larger system.

Travellers should compare total journey time, connection length, fare conditions and baggage charges. A new route creates choice, but it does not guarantee that every connection will be the fastest or cheapest option on every date.

Roanoke receives a direct Texas connection

A new link for Virginia’s Blue Ridge

American launched its Dallas Fort Worth to Roanoke flight on 4 June 2026. The airline announced a once-daily, year-round operation using a Bombardier CRJ-900.

Roanoke-Blacksburg Regional Airport now lists DFW among its nonstop destinations. The airport serves Virginia’s Blue Ridge region, including leisure, educational, business and visiting-friends-and-relatives markets.

The route provides a direct east-west connection between southwestern Virginia and North Texas. It also allows passengers from Roanoke to transfer through DFW towards other US and international destinations.

For inbound travellers, Roanoke acts as an air gateway to mountain scenery, outdoor recreation, communities along Virginia’s Blue Ridge and parts of the Blue Ridge Parkway region. Road transport remains necessary for many attractions, so visitors should plan car hire or other ground arrangements before arrival.

The service can support weekend tourism, longer outdoor holidays, university-related visits and corporate travel. Its year-round status provides greater continuity than the seasonal European additions.

Tourism already supports the regional economy

Official information published by Visit Virginia’s Blue Ridge showed that visitors generated US$882.2 million in direct spending in 2023 across the cities of Roanoke and Salem and the counties of Botetourt, Franklin and Roanoke.

The broader regional tourism impact reached approximately US$1.356 billion, representing growth of nearly seven per cent over 2022. Visitor activity supported 7,280 direct tourism jobs and produced almost US$43 million in local tax collections.

Spending was distributed across multiple categories:

Food and beverages: US$265.3 million

Transportation: US$235 million

Accommodation: US$179.4 million

Recreation: US$110.7 million

Retail: US$91.8 million

The data show that aviation connectivity affects more than airports. Visitors who arrive by air may spend money with hotels, restaurants, car-hire businesses, attractions, shops and outdoor recreation providers.

However, the figures predate the DFW route and must not be presented as benefits generated by it. They establish the size of the existing visitor economy against which the new service can eventually be evaluated.

Virginia’s statewide tourism industry provides further context

Virginia government planning information records US$35.1 billion in statewide visitor spending during 2024, 21 per cent above the 2019 level of US$29.1 billion.

The state received 44.7 million overnight visitors in 2024, also exceeding the pre-pandemic benchmark. Virginia’s tourism authority set an objective of reaching US$100 million in visitor spending per day, equivalent to US$36.5 billion annually.

A direct Roanoke–DFW route can assist this broader ambition by improving access from Texas and from cities connected through American’s hub. It may also make Virginia’s Blue Ridge more competitive for conferences, sporting events and leisure visitors who consider flight convenience when selecting destinations.

Yet air service alone cannot deliver tourism growth. Destination marketing, accommodation capacity, ground transport, pricing and the quality of visitor experiences determine whether improved access produces longer stays and higher spending.

DFW connecting model is central to the expansion

More than 230 American destinations from the hub

At the time of the European route launch, American said Athens and Zurich joined more than 230 nonstop destinations available from DFW through its operation. This scale explains why four routes can have implications far beyond eight individual cities.

A hub works by coordinating arrivals and departures into waves, commonly called banks. Passengers arrive from multiple origins, transfer inside the airport and depart for a second destination. The model helps airlines sustain routes that might not rely solely on passengers travelling between the two endpoint cities.

American introduced a 13-bank schedule at DFW in 2026. The carrier said the revised structure distributed more than 930 peak daily departures more evenly throughout the day.

According to the airline’s official May announcement, early results included fewer delays, better connections, fewer gate changes and improved baggage performance. Those are company-reported operational outcomes rather than independently audited conclusions, but they reveal the purpose of the schedule redesign.

For Athens, Zurich, Lincoln and Roanoke passengers, connection quality can be as important as the flight itself. A route may appear attractive on paper, yet a very short or extremely long layover can weaken the overall journey.

DFW remains one of the world’s largest airports

DFW handled more than 87.8 million passengers in 2024, according to the airport, representing growth of 7.4 per cent over 2023 and 17 per cent over 2019.

Airports Council International ranked DFW third globally for total passenger traffic in 2024. The airport’s growth rate was the highest among the three leading airports identified in that ranking: Atlanta, Dubai and DFW.

DFW has seven runways and a large terminal complex positioned between Dallas and Fort Worth. Its geographical location supports connections between the eastern and western United States and between domestic feeder markets and international services.

Strong traffic does not eliminate operational risks. Large hubs face weather disruption, air-traffic constraints, congestion and the possibility that delays in one bank will affect later departures. Travellers connecting at DFW should monitor the American Airlines application, airport information and any official travel alerts.

Major infrastructure spending underpins future expansion

DFW Forward represents a US$12 billion programme

DFW Airport is implementing a historic US$12 billion capital plan known as DFW Forward. The programme covers terminals, airfield facilities and road infrastructure.

The scale of this investment matters because continued route growth requires sufficient gate capacity, baggage infrastructure, passenger-processing facilities and access roads. Adding flights without expanding or modernising facilities can intensify congestion.

One of the most prominent projects is Terminal F. The airport described the planned facility as a US$4 billion development intended ultimately to provide 31 gates served entirely by American Airlines.

The terminal is also designed to increase capacity for international operations and widebody aircraft. Its planned facilities include parking, check-in, ticketing, security screening and baggage operations.

The first phase is expected to open with 15 gates in 2027. Because that date falls after the four routes began, the 2026 expansion is operating while the airport continues a major construction and modernisation programme.

Passengers should consult official airport guidance before travelling because construction can affect road access, parking, terminal movement and gate assignments.

New gates and redesigned facilities target the customer journey

American and DFW have pursued projects across the existing terminal system while Terminal F develops. These investments are designed to improve gate availability and prepare the hub for future demand.

The airport expects annual passenger traffic to exceed 100 million before 2030. This is a projection rather than a confirmed outcome, but it illustrates why additional infrastructure is being constructed now.

Growth presents both opportunity and pressure. More passengers can support expanded routes and regional spending. At the same time, airports must maintain security, baggage handling, accessibility, ground transport and passenger comfort.

For travel businesses, the implication is clear: DFW is not simply adding four isolated services. The routes fit within a much larger attempt to reinforce the airport as a global connecting platform.

Economic implications extend across North Texas

DFW Airport reports that it generates more than US$78 billion in annual economic impact for North Texas. Its official figures include approximately US$48 billion in supported payroll, 684,000 direct and indirect jobs, US$18 billion in visitor spending and US$8 billion in state and local tax revenue.

These totals represent the airport’s broad economic footprint. They should not be attributed specifically to American’s four new routes.

Each additional service can nevertheless contribute incrementally through airline employment, airport activity, tourism expenditure and stronger business links. International routes may also facilitate trade, investment and conference travel, while domestic routes improve connectivity between regional economies.

Athens and Zurich connect North Texas with established European tourism and commercial centres. Lincoln strengthens links with a state capital and major university market. Roanoke opens direct access to a regional economy with education, healthcare, manufacturing, technology and tourism activity.

Measuring the routes precise economic contribution would require information that was not publicly available in the reviewed official sources as of 4 August 2026. Relevant indicators would include passenger numbers, load factors, visitor origin, average spending, trip duration and the proportion of travellers connecting at DFW.

A responsible report should therefore identify potential economic channels without publishing an invented impact estimate.

Wider benefits for the travel trade

Tour operators gain new itinerary-building options

The routes create opportunities for tour operators and travel advisers to develop new products.

Athens can support classical Greece programmes, island combinations, culinary holidays and cultural tours. Zurich can form the starting point for rail-based Swiss holidays, Alpine itineraries and multi-country European journeys. Lincoln can be combined with Nebraska heritage, sporting and event travel. Roanoke can anchor Blue Ridge Parkway, outdoor adventure and mountain-region itineraries.

The strongest products will reflect each route’s actual schedule. A seasonal European flight requires travel dates that align with the operating window. Domestic itineraries must consider the arrival time, onward transport and availability of accommodation.

Travel sellers should also distinguish nonstop from direct and connecting travel. The four services are nonstop between DFW and the named destination, but many passengers will connect at DFW before or after that flight.

Meetings and business travel may benefit

Frequency and schedule consistency are particularly important for business travel. Lincoln’s twice-daily service offers greater flexibility than a single daily flight. Roanoke’s daily operation creates a direct link that did not previously exist in American’s published DFW network.

Zurich connects two significant business regions, although its limited summer window restricts year-round corporate usefulness. Athens combines government, business and leisure demand while also providing access to Greece’s wider economy.

Companies considering the routes should evaluate change policies, baggage terms, corporate contracts and alternative options during disruption. Seasonal service ending on a specified date requires particular care when planning return travel.

Smaller airports gain access to a global network

Lincoln and Roanoke illustrate the role of regional aviation in connecting smaller communities with international gateways.

Residents do not need every overseas destination to be served nonstop from their local airport. A reliable flight to a well-connected hub can provide practical access to many destinations through a single connection.

This model also creates inbound opportunity. Travellers from distant markets can reach Lincoln or Roanoke on one itinerary, potentially improving destination visibility and reducing the friction associated with separate tickets or long road transfers.

The effectiveness of the connection depends on fare competitiveness, schedule reliability and the time required to transfer at DFW.

What travellers should know before booking

Passengers considering any of the four services should verify the live timetable directly with American Airlines.

Important points include:

Athens is seasonal. Availability should be confirmed for the intended travel date.

Zurich was scheduled only until 4 August 2026. Travellers should not assume later service without official confirmation.

Lincoln operates twice daily and year-round under the published announcement.

Roanoke operates once daily and year-round under the published announcement.

Aircraft can change for operational reasons.

Flight frequency can be adjusted even after a route is announced.

International passengers must confirm passport, visa and entry requirements through official authorities.

Travellers connecting from an international arrival at DFW should allow time for immigration, customs, baggage procedures and security screening.

Baggage allowances depend on the fare, cabin, loyalty status and itinerary.

Construction at DFW may affect road access, parking or terminal movement.

Separately ticketed onward journeys may not carry the same protection as a single through-ticket.

American’s official travel alerts should be checked shortly before departure. DFW Airport also provides flight information, maps, parking details and security-wait information.

Policy and regulatory considerations

All four routes operate within established aviation regulatory systems. Domestic services are subject to US aviation and consumer-protection requirements. International services also involve bilateral traffic rights, border controls and destination entry rules.

The launch of a route does not alter a country’s immigration policy. US citizens travelling to Greece or Switzerland must check the latest official European and national requirements. European travellers entering the United States must confirm whether they require a visa or qualify to use the Visa Waiver Program and obtain the relevant authorisation.

Travellers should avoid relying on social-media summaries for entry requirements. Passport validity, permissible stay, travel authorisation and documentation rules can change independently of an airline schedule.

Consumer protections also vary by jurisdiction and circumstance. Cancellation, refund and rebooking rights may depend on which airline cancelled the flight, the reason for disruption and the laws applying to the journey.

Environmental implications require balanced assessment

New flights increase connectivity but also add aviation activity. Long-haul services use substantially more fuel per departure than regional flights, although emissions per passenger depend on aircraft type, seating configuration, load factor and distance.

DFW has published environmental and sustainability programmes as part of its wider airport planning. American Airlines also reports sustainability initiatives, including fleet renewal and sustainable aviation fuel agreements.

These programmes should not be used to claim that a new route has no environmental cost. Sustainable aviation fuel remains limited in supply, and emissions reductions depend on feedstock, production methods and actual use.

Travellers who consider environmental impact can compare direct and connecting itineraries, aircraft information and available surface-transport alternatives. A nonstop flight may avoid an additional take-off and landing compared with a connection, but route-specific emissions still require credible calculation.

Future outlook for American Airlines Dallas routes

The four additions strengthen DFW role as American’s primary hub, but their longer-term performance will depend on demand and operational results.

The Lincoln and Roanoke services have the clearest continuity because American announced them as year-round routes. Their success will likely depend on a mixture of local passengers, visitors and connecting traffic.

Athens serves an established summer market and forms part of American’s wider expansion towards Greece. Its future schedule will depend on commercial decisions that the airline must confirm officially.

Zurich was explicitly limited to 4 August 2026. Its return cannot be assumed. The airline may evaluate passenger demand, yields, operational requirements and fleet availability before making later scheduling decisions.

DFW expanding facilities create room for future network development. Terminal F, new gates and the redesigned bank structure are intended to support growth, particularly in American’s operation.

For destinations, retaining air service requires coordinated effort. Airports, tourism boards, businesses and event organisers can help generate demand through marketing and itinerary development. However, public claims should distinguish promotional ambition from confirmed traffic performance.

The most credible conclusion as of 4 August 2026 is that American successfully brought four new DFW links into its 2026 network. Two broaden domestic access on a year-round basis. One creates seasonal access to Greece. The other provided a defined summer link with Switzerland. Together, they illustrate how a large hub can simultaneously serve global tourism and smaller regional markets.

Conclusion

American Airlines Dallas routes have grown to reach places through four different connections to Athens, Zurich, Lincoln and Roanoke. These new trips to Europe open up ways for people to travel for fun or work. At the time the flights inside the country give Nebraska and Virginia better access to the American Airlines global hub all year long. The big size of DFW, a flight schedule and a multi billion-dollar infrastructure programme are helping this growth happen. However you should always check the flight dates before you go. This is important because the Zurich flights are set to end on 4 August 2026. These American Airlines Dallas routes offer chances for travel but we will have to look at future data, on spending and passenger numbers to see how much these American Airlines Dallas routes truly help the economy.

text:
ASTM D8615 provides an automated optical-fibre method for measuring aviation fuel freezing point, reducing operator judgement while leaving laboratories to manage method validation and specification requirements.

Freezing-point testing is a routine part of aviation fuel quality control, but the measurement has traditionally involved a significant degree of operator judgement.

ASTM D8615-26 provides an automated alternative.

Find your test and measurement instrument in our international directory.

The standard covers the determination of the temperature below which solid hydrocarbon crystals may form in aviation turbine fuels, using an automatic coaxial optical-fibre method.

The method is now available as the 2026 edition of ASTM D8615, superseding the 2025 edition.

For fuel laboratories, the significance is less about replacing one instrument overnight and more about how automated measurement can change the workflow around a familiar test.

From visual judgement to optical measurement

The conventional ASTM D2386 method relies on manual observation of the formation and disappearance of hydrocarbon crystals.

ASTM says D8615 eliminates most of the operator time and judgement associated with this manual approach. Results are reported to the nearest 0.1 °C.

The new method uses coaxial optical fibres to detect the relevant change during controlled cooling and warming.

Automation can therefore reduce the subjective element of the measurement and create a more consistent sequence of operations.

That has practical implications for laboratories handling repeated batches of aviation fuel samples.

The standard does not automatically replace D2386

One important qualification is explicit in the standard.

Where a fuel specification requires ASTM D2386, D8615 must not simply be substituted. ASTM states that D8615 should not replace D2386 where the specification specifically calls for the latter method.

This is important when considering instrument purchases.

A laboratory cannot assume that the availability of an automated method means every existing D2386 requirement can immediately be transferred to the new procedure.

Method selection remains linked to the specification, customer requirement and applicable quality system.

Precision and validation

ASTM D8615-26 defines a reporting range of −71.2 °C to −36.5 °C for the application of the stated precision values.

The apparatus itself has a wider measuring range, from −80 °C to 20 °C, but ASTM notes that precision has not been established across the entire instrument range.

The precision data behind the method came from an interlaboratory study involving 12 laboratories and 15 materials.

For laboratory managers, this reinforces a familiar principle: automation does not remove the need for method validation.

A new analyser still needs to be incorporated into the laboratory’s QA/QC system. Analysts need to understand calibration, maintenance, verification and any differences between the automated method and the laboratory’s existing procedure.

Relevance to SAF testing

The method also has relevance beyond conventional aviation turbine fuels.

ASTM has stated that the standard can be used to test sustainable aviation turbine fuels.

The underlying measurement remains important because freezing point is linked to the behaviour of fuel at the low temperatures encountered during flight.

As fuel composition changes, laboratories will need analytical methods capable of providing reliable measurements across different fuel formulations.

This does not mean that ASTM D8615 resolves every analytical challenge associated with sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

It does, however, provide another standardised route for an established fuel quality parameter.

What changes in the laboratory?

For laboratories considering the method, the main questions are practical.

Can the existing specification be tested using D8615? Does the laboratory need to maintain D2386 capability? What validation evidence is required before reporting results? How will the new instrument fit into existing calibration and quality control procedures?

Those questions are likely to matter more than the simple fact that the test is automated.

ASTM D8615-26 provides laboratories with a more automated approach to freezing-point measurement, but method compliance remains dependent on the specification being applied.

The shift is therefore not from manual testing to automatic testing in isolation.

title: The Real Reason Why Aircraft Recyclers Dread The Retirement Of The Airbus A350 & Boeing 787
authors: Daniel S Osipov, Aaron Spray, Jack McGarity
description:

The metal can then either be reused in the production of spare aircraft parts or for non-aviation applications.
As such, CFRP components are largely discarded during disassembly, which will become a much larger issue as the majority of CFRP aircraft age out.

In addition to the economic aspect of recycling aircraft parts, there's also the environmental component.
text:
CFRP, short for carbon fiber reinforced polymer, has become the new standard for commercial aircraft construction. Lighter and stronger than traditional aircraft aluminum alloys, manufacturers have increasingly been incorporating the material, also known as composites. By weight, the Boeing 777 is 8% composites, while the Airbus A320 is 10% and the A380 is 25%. Meanwhile, the 787 Dreamliner and A350 XWB are majority composite by weight and over 80% composite by construction.

The use of composites has allowed manufacturers to design smaller, more fuel-efficient aircraft with longer ranges, essentially revolutionizing ultra-long-haul travel. However, while the use of CFRP is beneficial today, it poses a major problem for aircraft recyclers who recycle planes at the end of their lives. With some 787s and A350s now over ten years old, now is the time to begin exploring solutions on how to recycle carbon-composite airliners when they reach 20 or 30 years old.

The Challenge With Recycling CFRP Airliners

When a 767 is scrapped, the aircraft is first drained of liquids such as hydraulic fluids and then washed before being lubricated. Explosives from the emergency exit slides are deactivated, the air ducts are sealed, and a protective coat of paint is then applied before the aircraft is dismantled. Parts in high demand are then reused on the second-hand market, while the rest of the metal components are recycled for other use. Non-metal parts with no recycling value are discarded.

The most common metals recycled are aluminum and titanium alloys. Based on their composition, the metal alloys are sorted and then melted together to form a single alloy. The metal can then either be reused in the production of spare aircraft parts or for non-aviation applications. These can vary widely, ranging from automotive parts to consumer goods. In 2024, Delta Air Lines and American Express issued a limited-edition SkyMiles card made in part from recycled metal from the carrier's long-retired Boeing 747 fleet.

Carbon composite parts can be reused on the spare parts market, but recycling the material itself is more difficult. The primary component of CFRP is carbon fiber, which can be used in multiple applications. The challenge, however, is that the aviation industry has yet to develop comprehensive solutions for separating the materials that make up a CFRP component and using them for future aviation parts. As such, CFRP components are largely discarded during disassembly, which will become a much larger issue as the majority of CFRP aircraft age out.

Current Solutions For These Planes

In 2025, Airbus signed an agreement with French deeptech recycling firm Fairmat to study recycling technologies for CFRP airliners. Airbus currently produces the A350, which is 53% CFRP by weight and uses the material for a majority of the plane's construction, along with the A220, which is 46% CFRP by weight and uses the material for its wings and fuselage. As such, Airbus has a significant stake in ensuring that its planes can be recycled when they age out.

The main purpose of the study is to explore how to extract the carbon fiber, which is the most valuable part of a CFRP component, without damaging its strength. This is difficult because the fibers are bound in resin, and the study aims to understand the conditions required to extract them without compromising their integrity. What's more, the study aims to assess the suitability of the extracted fiber for use in aviation. Currently, the two parties are focusing on the Airbus A350, examining its wing and keel beam pieces.

This is the bigger challenge, as materials used on aircraft are subject to intense physical stress and must pass strict certification requirements. Fairmat, which specializes in recycling carbon fiber, has developed Infinity Recycling, a technology that uses a low-energy plasma process, mechanical precision, and advanced software. However, while the firm has experience with Infinity Recycling for composites, it's yet to produce carbon fiber suitable for aviation.

Why Recycled Materials Are More Common Than You Realize

A majority of a retired airliner's value comes from its engines. Parts like an APU or landing gear can also be valuable, sometimes recertified and sold as spares, or broken down for resale. Meanwhile, the rest of an aircraft's components are recycled. Recycled metal is desirable because the process for creating aluminum alloys is energy-intensive and therefore expensive. This is even more so for titanium alloys, which are desirable for their increased strength despite being heavier than aluminum.

This same market will exist for cheaper CFRP components, which are stronger, more fire-resistant, more resistant to corrosion, and have higher fatigue limits than metal alloys. Currently, CFRP airliners are being produced in large numbers, but they remain expensive to purchase, and the potential for reused parts or materials will be instrumental in ensuring their viability decades from now, once they're out of production.

In addition to the economic aspect of recycling aircraft parts, there's also the environmental component. Recycling metal components reduces the need to create new alloys, thereby lowering greenhouse gas emissions. The same is true for composites. What's more, CFRP is non-biodegradable, meaning it persists in landfills, while incineration releases toxic gases into the environment. As such, it's within the aviation industry's interests to ensure that solutions are available to facilitate widespread CFRP recycling.

The In-Production Airliners That Are Using CFRP

Carbon composites have long been used in the aviation industry, but on a relatively small scale. As previously mentioned, the A350 uses CFRP for the majority of its construction (over 80% in volume), while the A220 uses the material primarily for its wings and empennage. Boeing, meanwhile, has been delivering the 787 for almost 15 years, which was the world's first majority composite airliner. By weight, the 787 is roughly 50% composites, while by volume it's roughly 80%, similar to the A350.

The 787 is Boeing's only majority-composite airliner, but it's also working to certify the 777X, which features new CFRP wings. In addition, some new derivatives of older airliners feature an increased use of CFRP; the out-of-production 747-8 features added CFRP components in its wings and engine nacelles, and the same is true for the A330neo. With its bespoke CFRP wing, however, the 777X is the best example of a new aircraft variant with a much higher CFRP content than before.

However, while composites are the future, it's unclear how widely new airliners will use the material in the short term. Currently, Airbus is actively studying the development of a replacement for the A320neo, while Boeing's next airliner will be a replacement for the 737 MAX. These planes will primarily be used on short-to-medium-haul flights, where the reduced weight from composites has less benefit. The A220 doesn't use CFRP in its fuselage, and composites for the wings haven't provided a clear benefit for the program, given the small fuel savings and high manufacturing costs.

The Aviation Industry's Sustainability Efforts

The image that typically comes into mind when discussing aircraft recycling is the reuse of scrap metal and, in the future, CFRP components. However, airliners also have interiors that need attention. Rather than throw away the seat covers, Southwest Airlines launched an initiative in 2013 to upcycle the leather seat covers of its retired airliners. The project involves partnering with non-profit organizations to turn the leather into consumer products and has been hugely successful.

In addition to the industry's recycling efforts, it's also working on directly reducing the environmental impact of flying. On the one hand, the use of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is considered a key method to decarbonize the industry, as it leads to lower carbon emissions than traditional jet fuel, and SAF production uses renewable waste. On the other hand, the industry is actively exploring new propulsion technology, such as hydrogen-powered engines or batteries.

In addition to these, the industry is also tackling what many believe is one of aviation's biggest contributors to global warming: contrails. These are essentially man-made miniature clouds that trap heat emitted by the Earth, and American Airlines is actively leading an effort to adjust flight paths to reduce contrail production. While debate persists over the full impact of contrails, the industry is taking the issue seriously. In addition, the use of SAF is believed to also reduce contrails.

title: Utility Businesses maintain steady development Growth Businesses demonstrate strong momentum
description:
-- The Hong Kong and China Gas Company Limited (stock code: 0003, hereinafter referred to as “the Group”) has announced its 2026 interim results.
In the Hong Kong utility business, the supply of feedstocks for gas production remained unaffected by the external environment.
However, high temperatures and a surge in outbound tourism among local residents weighed on residential gas sales.
As of the end of June, Hong Kong gas sales reached 14.4 billion MJ (equivalent to approximately 410 million cubic metres of natural gas), down 3.5% year-on-year.
In the first half of 2026, VENEX successfully completed Hong Kong’s first container terminal bunkering, completing a fully integrated supply chain from northern China to Hong Kong.
text:
-- The Hong Kong and China Gas Company Limited (stock code: 0003, hereinafter referred to as “the Group”) has announced its 2026 interim results. In the first half of this year, facing international energy market volatility and economic challenges, the Group’s utility businesses demonstrated strong resilience through improved efficiency and business restructuring; meanwhile, growth businesses achieved breakthrough progress, with operating profit during the period surging by 3 times year-on-year. Overall, the Group recorded a rise of 19% in operating profit after tax for the period to HK$4.746 billion, while profit attributable to shareholders grew by 23% to HK$3.64 billion.

In the Hong Kong utility business, the supply of feedstocks for gas production remained unaffected by the external environment. Benefitting from the gradual recovery of the tourism sector, gas consumption among commercial customers, including the catering and hospitality industries, recorded a modest increase. However, high temperatures and a surge in outbound tourism among local residents weighed on residential gas sales. As of the end of June, Hong Kong gas sales reached 14.4 billion MJ (equivalent to approximately 410 million cubic metres of natural gas), down 3.5% year-on-year. The Group had adjusted its standard town gas tariff and the monthly maintenance charge, effective from 1st August 2026.

In the mainland utility businesses, amid the economic slowdown, the impact of a mild winter, and property market adjustments, the Group actively capitalised on policy tailwinds in energy transition, urban renewal and ageing pipeline network upgrades, while pressing ahead with its “Gas+” integrated energy business, driving a rise in gas sales volume. Cost pass-through arrangements were steadily implemented during the period, bringing the dollar margin for city gas to RMB0.55 per cubic metre, a further improvement of RMB0.01 per cubic metre year-on-year, driving steady profit growth in the overall gas business. The water and environmental businesses delivered sustainable growth, with water sales and sewage treatment volume reaching 800 million tonnes, up 2%, and solid waste treatment volume reaching 830,000 tonnes, an increase of 5%.

In sustainable aviation fuel (“SAF”), EcoCeres, Inc. (“EcoCeres”), incubated by the Group, which remains a strategic shareholder, successfully commenced trial production at its Malaysia plant in 2025. Sales in the first half of 2026 were strong, reaching 320,000 tonnes, approximately double the level recorded a year earlier. EcoCeres successfully extended its SAF supply agreement with British Airways until the end of 2030. Furthermore, it signed an investment letter of intent with the Dongguan Municipal Government to establish a complete SAF and hydrotreated vegetable oil (“HVO”) value chain in the Greater Bay Area with annual capacity of about 450,000 tonnes. This will bring EcoCeres’s total annual capacity to 1.22 million tonnes.

In green methanol, VENEX, a joint venture under the Group, actively expanded its production capacity; the Inner Mongolia project is ramping up capacity to 300,000 tonnes following its retrofitting. Construction of new Foshan Plant will commence this year with planned capacity of 200,000 tonnes, establishing a strategic dual-base footprint spanning northern and southern China, with total planned capacity of 500,000 tonnes. In the first half of 2026, VENEX successfully completed Hong Kong’s first container terminal bunkering, completing a fully integrated supply chain from northern China to Hong Kong. VENEX also received one of the first certifications under the Country’s Global Sustainable Transport Certification (GSTC) scheme.

In the renewable energy business, new grid-connected distributed photovoltaic capacity reached 0.2 GW during the period, bringing cumulative installed capacity to 3 GW; photovoltaic electricity sales increased by 12% year-on-year to 1.32 billion kWh; and electricity trading sales volume doubled to 7.23 billion kWh. During the period, the Group successfully launched an institutional REIT and a quasi-REIT to raise approximately RMB900 million, bringing cumulative financing to RMB5.5 billion for active investment in business-related projects. The scale of Assets under Management (“AuM”) increased by 0.66 GW year-on-year to 1.5 GW, and the Group remains well-positioned across three key growth areas: integrated PV-storage, independent energy storage and direct green power supply.

In the extended businesses, Towngas Lifestyle, a Group’s subsidiary, accelerated its transformation into a “home concierge service” model by leveraging the massive market opportunities presented by the Group’s 47 million city-gas customers, and unified its kitchen appliance brand under Mia Cucina. On the mainland, trade-in sales for the smart kitchen appliance business grew 17% year-on-year to RMB200 million, while the heating engineering business grew 14% year-on-year to RMB120 million. In Hong Kong, smart kitchen revenue in the first half reached HK$870 million, up 7% year-on-year.

The year 2026 marks the opening year of the national 15th Five-Year Plan, with green fuels included in the national strategy for the first time. In close alignment with national strategic objectives, the Group will capitalise on its competitive advantages to strategically deploy its advanced technologies and management excellence across the Greater Bay Area, as well as in Central Asia and other countries along the Belt and Road, to expand its international new energy footprint.

The Board recommended maintaining an interim dividend of HK12 cents per share.

For details of the results, please refer to the 2026 Interim Results Announcement published on the Company’s website at www.towngas.com and the HKEXnews website at www.hkexnews.hk.

title: Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) — A Practitioner's Guide - Kingdom Jets
description:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is jet fuel manufactured from bio-feedstocks (used cooking oils, agricultural residues, energy crops) or synthetic pathways (power-to-liquid, electrofuels).
Typical bio-based SAF delivers verified 70-80% lifecycle emissions reduction vs. conventional Jet-A.
Three certification frameworks dominate the verified SAF market in 2026: CORSIA-approved SAF: meets ICAO's Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme criteria.
Major business jet manufacturers have made formal SAF commitments and approved use protocols: Gulfstream: all current production approved for 50% SAF blends.
Embraer: Praetor and Phenom family approved for 50% SAF; Embraer's commercial aviation sustainability efforts inform business jet protocols.
text:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is jet fuel manufactured from bio-feedstocks (used cooking oils, agricultural residues, energy crops) or synthetic pathways (power-to-liquid, electrofuels). The fuel is chemically equivalent to conventional Jet-A and certified for use in current turbine engines at blends up to 50% without modification, and up to 100% with select operator approvals.

Lifecycle emissions reduction depends on feedstock and production pathway. Typical bio-based SAF delivers verified 70-80% lifecycle emissions reduction vs. conventional Jet-A. Synthetic power-to-liquid SAF can deliver 95%+ reduction when produced with renewable electricity. The reductions are measured on a well-to-wake basis, not just combustion emissions.

SAF availability at business-aviation FBOs has expanded substantially: roughly 35 major FBOs globally as of mid-2026, up from 5 in 2020. Strongest coverage: European hubs (Farnborough, Geneva, Nice, Zurich, Vienna, Munich, Bordeaux); US (Van Nuys, Burbank, San Francisco, Westchester, Teterboro); Middle East (Dubai DWC, Riyadh growing); Asia-Pacific (Singapore Seletar leading).

Most available blends are 30-40%; some FBOs offer 50% and a small number offer 100% SAF for select operators. The blend percentage is normally at FBO discretion and operator agreement.

For most private aviation users, the right approach in 2026 is: default to 30% SAF blend on supported routes (modest premium, meaningful emissions reduction, demand pull scales supply). Pay for verified carbon removal (DAC, biochar, ocean alkalinity) on non-SAF flights. Avoid avoidance-credit carbon offsetting — the scientific community has moved firmly toward removal over avoidance.

For higher-utilisation operators, structured SAF procurement contracts at scale can lock in current pricing and access. Several manufacturers and operators now offer SAF-bundled hour packages.

Not all SAF claims are equally credible. Three certification frameworks dominate the verified SAF market in 2026:

CORSIA-approved SAF: meets ICAO's Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme criteria. Required for emissions accounting under CORSIA. Lifecycle emissions reductions independently verified by accredited third parties.

ISCC-EU (International Sustainability and Carbon Certification): dominant in European market. Verifies feedstock sustainability, supply chain integrity, and lifecycle emissions per EU Renewable Energy Directive criteria.

IATA Sustainability Verification Programme: aviation-industry framework providing verified emissions accounting for both SAF and removal credits. Increasingly recognised across business aviation.

Reputable operators provide certification documentation on request. Uncertified SAF claims should be treated sceptically — the price premium typical for SAF is meaningless if the lifecycle benefit is unverified.

SAF is produced via multiple pathways with different feedstock dependencies and lifecycle emissions profiles:

HEFA (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids): primary current production pathway. Uses bio-feedstocks (used cooking oils, animal fats, agricultural residues). Mature production technology, growing capacity. Lifecycle emissions reduction: 70–80%.

FT-SPK (Fischer-Tropsch Synthetic Paraffinic Kerosene): produces SAF from gasified biomass or municipal waste. Strong lifecycle reductions; production technology mature but capacity limited.

ATJ (Alcohol-to-Jet): produces SAF from sugar-fermentation alcohols. Growing production capacity, especially in Brazil. Lifecycle reductions vary by feedstock.

Power-to-Liquid (PtL / e-fuels): synthetic SAF produced from CO2 and renewable hydrogen. Lifecycle reductions of 95%+ achievable with fully-renewable electricity. Production capacity nascent; pricing premium substantial.

For most current bookings, the SAF you purchase is HEFA-pathway. PtL availability is growing but expensive. The certification framework matters more than the specific pathway from a verification standpoint.

Major business jet manufacturers have made formal SAF commitments and approved use protocols:

Gulfstream: all current production approved for 50% SAF blends. 100% SAF approval programme underway for G700/G800. Gulfstream maintains corporate SAF procurement contracts for company demo flights and factory deliveries.

Bombardier: similar 50% blend approval across current production. Maintains industry-leading sustainability reporting in their annual reports.

Dassault: Falcon family approved for 50% SAF; corporate sustainability commitments include carbon-removal partnerships.

Embraer: Praetor and Phenom family approved for 50% SAF; Embraer's commercial aviation sustainability efforts inform business jet protocols.

Cessna / Textron: Citation family approved across the range. Textron Aviation has structured SAF procurement for new aircraft delivery flights.

Manufacturer SAF programmes are increasingly meaningful in fleet decisions — particularly for corporate flight departments with ESG reporting requirements.

text:
Izumiotsu City and Takaishi City in Osaka Prefecture have started collecting and recycling household used cooking oil, in a partnership to turn household waste into renewable energy.

In Japan, households typically dispose of used tempura or cooking oil by solidifying it with chemical coagulants or soaking it in paper before discarding it as combustible waste. This disposal method demands time and incurs financial costs for households purchasing coagulants. It also carries the risk of leaks and odours in the rubbish, while completely wasting a reusable material.

The new programme provides a more efficient alternative. Residents pour their cooled used oil into standard PET bottles and drop them off at designated collection points. Because Izumiotsu and Takaishi are compact and adjacent cities where citizens frequently cross municipal boundaries for shopping and commuting, the local governments designed the system to be borderless. Residents use drop-off locations in either city interchangeably, allowing them to recycle their oil during routine errands. This lowers the barrier to participation returning resources into the circular economy

Uedayushi Co., Ltd. handles the recycling process. The collected oil undergoes processing to become biodiesel fuel and serves as a raw material for Sustainable Aviation Fuel. Furthermore, the facility recycles the PET bottles used to transport the oil. This guarantees that the transport container does not become new rubbish, effectively circulating both the oil and the plastic. ENEOS Corporation collaborates on the scheme to promote the collection of this oil specifically for future aviation fuel production.

This infrastructure transforms a cumbersome household chore into an accessible civic action. By enabling citizens to drop off oil during their routine shopping trips, the initiative lowers the barrier to participation in the circular economy. This domestic resource circulation shifts reliance away from imported energy, proving that everyday household waste holds the power to fuel future transport networks.
